newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief outraged at Somalia atrocities.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief outraged at Somalia atrocities.

text.p: With Canadian, Italian and Belgian troops under U.N. command accused of atrocities in Somalia, Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Monday expressed outrage and said such actions were unacceptable.
"I have been advised of alleged atrocities commited while on duty in Somalia by U.N. peacekeeping soldiers," he said in a statement.

"I am appalled and outraged by these actions which are unacceptable and counter to everything peacekeeping stands for," said Annan, who served as U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping through most of the ill-fated Somalia operation, beginning in 1993.
His comments were the first on the growing controversies since he became secretary-general in January.

Two years after U.N. forces withdrew from Somalia, stories of atrocities are still emerging. Belgium is trying two soldiers on charges of roasting a live Somali child over an open fire in 1993 and Italian papers recently released photos showing an officer applying electrodes to the hands and genitals of a young, naked Somali man.
And Canada, once the bedrock of U.N. peacekeeping, discovered that members of a parachute unit in 1993 murdered a Somali teenager and photographed themselves smiling next to the corpse.
In each case U.N. officials said they did not know of the abuses. If they had they could not prosecute the offenders but insist their countries send them home for trial.

Since Somalia, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said, officials were more vigilant, and in Mozambique soldiers were sent home for patronising child prostitutes even before a U.N. report emerged on the subject.

Annan added: "While soldiers are under the command of their own superior officer, I wish to assure that every possible effort will be made on the part of the United Nations to ensure that such incidents do not recur."
"These soldiers are now being held to account by their ... governments and will be prosecuted in accordance with the law," he said.

Peacekeeping forces, cobbled together from various countries, are under the jurisdiction of their national commanders. But a general from a country contributing troops is named overall U.N. force commander.

Abuses by peacekeepers first came to light in Cambodia, where both civilian and military officials were accused of harassing women, widescale prostitution and drunken behaviour. Bulgaria was singled out frequently as the worst offender. But in public U.N. officials brushed off complaints there.

In Bosnia, the black market was at an all time high and U.N. troops were accused of going to or drinking near brothels run by Serbs with captive Bosnian or Croatian women. Few investigations were publicised and those that were found relatively minor abuses.
Some countries are known to take immediate action. Bangladeshi soldiers are said to be disciplined and any infraction is punished by a quick trip home.
